title: Why Gallup's Numbers Are Dubious
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian challenges the authority of Gallup's annual State of the Global Workplace engagement figure, arguing that the Q12 instrument measures something narrower and more commercial than the headline claims. He sets out five flaws: the Q12 began as a workplace conditions audit rather than an engagement measure, its correlations with business outcomes are weak (r between 0.057 and 0.191), the methodology is proprietary and not peer reviewed, the questions are culturally American yet applied in 160 countries, and the vendor also sells the remedy. He then compares Gallup's 21 percent global engagement with other providers who report 70 to 83 percent using different definitions. Global engagement has moved only from 12 to 20 percent in sixteen years, which he reads as evidence of a structural ceiling in the instrument. His conclusion is not that the data is worthless but that it deserves far more scepticism from leaders and HR teams.
points: The Q12 is better understood as a proxy for managerial quality and working conditions than as a measure of the multi-dimensional construct of engagement.
Gallup's own meta-analysis shows correlations with business outcomes that explain only about 0.3 to 3.6 percent of variance, a modest association rather than a transformational mechanism.
Because the formula is proprietary and unreviewed, and the same company sells the interventions, the framing forms a closed commercial loop.
Different providers report anywhere from 21 to 83 percent engagement because they define the construct differently, so leaders should ask what a number actually measures.
Sixteen years and billions of spend moved the global figure just eight points, which suggests the instrument has a structural ceiling rather than that management has universally failed.
quotes: The Q12 began life in the 1990s as a workplace conditions audit. It was a tool for assessing management practices and basic job needs. At no point were the twelve questions substantially rewritten. What changed was the label.
This matters because it means that Gallup’s ‘engagement’ score is actually a proxy for managerial quality - which is useful, but is not what it says on the tin.
Correlations in this range explain between 0.3% and 3.6% of the variance in business outcomes. The remaining 96–99% is explained by other factors.

In academic research, this would be disqualifying. The peer review process (in which independent scientists scrutinise methodology, analysis, and conclusions) is the mechanism by which science separates reliable findings from artefacts of method.
Gallup has administered this question, unchanged, across 160 countries. Its cross-cultural equivalence testing is not publicly available.
These are the result of measuring different things and calling them all ‘engagement’.
The way engagement is defined by the Q12 produces low scores by construction, and that the absolute level of 20–23% tells you more about the instrument than it does about the workforce.

The engagement industry’s most cited number is an instrument with modest correlations, opaque methodology, and cultural assumptions baked in from 1990s America. As such, it deserves to be used with considerably more care.
